subject: hedgehog
pitch: A plump hedgehog out on an autumn evening walk. A dome of spines in chestnut brown with cream tips, a soft fawn face with a pointed, twitchy snout, a shiny black button nose, tiny round ears and bright beady eyes. Little pink paws, and a single red maple leaf stuck on its spines like a trophy.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module using the SDK to model a hedgehog at realistic scale, roughly 25cm long and 12cm tall, working out the joint hierarchy with positions and orientations based on the available builder API.

I'm sketching how to use chains, sweeps, and parts for the body shape, and deciding to stick with primitive geometries and simple colors rather than riskier texture/decal features whose signatures I'm unsure of. For the spines, I'm thinking of scattering spike geometry across the back surface using the surface/scatter functions to create that signature dome of quills.

Right, so spike produces geometry that inherits bone placement, then gets placed via part without an explicit "at" since it already carries position data from the hit or sweep point. I'll call spike with the hit as both base and direction reference, then pass that geometry straight into part with a color.

Now I'm thinking through the body structure: the hedgehog as a chain of joints from hips to neck to head with a snout, body center sitting around y=0.07, overall length near 0.25m, dome height about 0.12, with the model oriented facing +Z.

I'm sketching a spine chain running from the rump to the shoulder to the head, then sweeping that path with a constant radius to form the body surface — though I'll need lofting instead if I want tapering at the ends. Then I plan to scatter spine points across that surface, filtering hits to the upper dome region so quills only appear on top, not underneath.

Since field names like axis and at on hit frames are uncertain, I'm considering a more deterministic approach instead: using surf.nearest(p) to snap predefined dome grid points to the actual surface, which avoids guessing at unclear API fields entirely.

I'll generate spine points on an ellipsoid shell around the body center, slightly offset outward so nearest() finds the true surface, excluding the face and underside regions. Aiming for roughly 170 spines across 14 rings of 12, keeping total part count comfortably under budget.

For coloring, I'm deciding to make most spines chestnut brown with about 30% randomly colored cream to give a two-tone texture, since computing a true tip-offset point without known helper functions is unreliable. I'll just call spike with the hit point as both base and direction reference, letting the frame logic derive orientation from the axis.

Now I'm moving to the face: the head will be a scaled sphere part for the fawn-colored ellipsoid shape, and the snout will extend forward as either a sweep or scaled sphere. I'm working out how to orient a cone geometry so its point aims in the +Z direction, reasoning through the rotation math to map the cone's default +Y tip to +Z via a rotateX transform.

Small details come next: ears, black eyes with a white highlight dot, a black nose sphere at the snout tip, and tiny pink paw ellipsoids positioned under the front and back legs. I'm also figuring out how to build a maple-leaf shape as an extruded 2D outline, generating a 10-point star pattern with alternating long and short radii at 36-degree intervals to approximate five pointed lobes.

I'm positioning the leaf flat on top of the hedgehog's spines near the dome's peak, choosing the extrusion directions so the leaf lies roughly horizontal with a slight tilt to look naturally stuck among the spikes.

Now I'm checking that all legs and paws rest properly at ground level (y=0), confirming the body sweep radius and leg dimensions line up so the bottom of the paws touch zero exactly, and the overall hedgehog stays compact at about 0.3 units long. I'm also settling on the color palette—chestnut, cream, fawn, black, pink, red, white—assigning fawn to the belly sweep since the spines will cover the dome, then placing small black and white spheres for beady eyes near the head joint.

Now I'm working out the snout and nose geometry, positioning the cone and nose sphere so the tip lands around z=0.22, sizing the head sphere with a slight squash for shape, and placing small flattened ear spheres in a darker fawn tone. I'm also defining the ellipsoid boundaries for the body so I can generate spine placement points across rows of latitude while keeping the face area clear of spines.

I'll use 7 rows by 14 columns of spines with randomized jitter in angle and position, varying spine length and radius slightly, and giving some tips a cream color for variation. Each spike gets positioned at its base point with direction based on the outward surface normal so they angle naturally away from the body.

I'm wrestling with how `b.part()` handles positioning when geometry is already computed in model-space coordinates versus needing explicit `at`/`bone` parameters — since the spike geometry inherits its placement from the hit point on the body surface, I'll likely omit explicit bone binding and let it default, trusting that passing just geometry and color works when the geometry is already in model coordinates.

I'm sketching the skeleton: a root "body" joint, then a "spine" chain of joints running front-to-back, which I'll sweep with a tube of radius 0.062 for the torso. Then I'm placing the head as a part positioned near the spine's front end, adding a snout cone rotated and offset forward, and planning the paws as simple sphere parts rather than swept chains.

For the paws, I'm positioning pink spheres near the front and back feet, squashing them slightly flat and elongated so they read as little pads, letting them auto-attach to the nearest bone. For the leaf accent, I'm adding a thin spike stem rising from the top of the body, then extruding a maple-leaf outline on top of it, tilting the leaf's orientation vectors so it sits naturally rather than flat, and sizing it around 4.5cm across to look proportional to the rest of the figure. Now I'm working out the leaf outline itself, placing lobe tips and valley points around a circle at alternating angles to form the classic five-lobed maple shape.

Finally I'm positioning the eyes as small spheres with white highlight dots, calculating their placement on the head's curved surface so they sit right at the correct depth given the head sphere's squashed radius.

Still writing component setup...

I'm realizing the chain needs a root joint first, so I'll create a hips joint before building the spine chain, then loop over rows and columns to generate the spine geometry with varying angles.

I need to fix the coordinate parametrization so spines wrap correctly around the body's long axis rather than the vertical axis — using polar angle from the top pole combined with azimuth around the y-axis to properly cover the back and flanks of the dome shape.

Then for each sampled point I find the nearest surface hit using the sweep body's surface handle, and place a spike primitive there with randomized length and a chance of cream versus chestnut coloring.

Now I'm adding the stem and leaf: a thin spike for the stem rising above the spine-covered area, topped with an extruded leaf shape oriented diagonally, keeping thickness at default since exact extrude options are uncertain. I'll skip vein details and move on to placing the eyes and nose.

Building out the head: a scaled fawn-colored sphere for the base, a rotated cone for the snout (checking the rotation math so the tip points forward correctly), a small black nose sphere, black eye spheres with tiny white highlight dots offset slightly forward, and ears as scaled spheres with pink inner spheres for the interior detail.

Adding paws now — front and back feet as stretched spheres positioned near the ground, pink-toned. Skipping a mouth and whiskers to keep things simple, then finishing up with just the code output.
